name: Teufelberger tygra 16-Strand Climbing Rope
title: Teufelberger tygra 16-Strand Climbing Rope
meta: Teufelberger tygra is a firm 16-strand climbing rope for MRS and SRS work. How it handles, which hitches and devices suit it, and how to care for it.
tagline: A firm, round 16-strand climbing line for climbers who run both MRS and SRS.
summary: Teufelberger tygra is a 16-strand climbing rope built to stay round and firm, so it runs cleanly through friction hitches and mechanical devices alike. It suits climbers who switch between moving-rope and stationary-rope setups through the week.
highlights: 16-strand construction with a firm, round profile
Works with friction hitches and many mechanical devices
Low stretch for efficient ascent on SRS
Common in eye-spliced lengths for climbing systems
Made by an established European rope maker

body.h: How tygra works on the job
p: Tygra is built for climbers who want one line that behaves on a hitch and in a device. The cover is tight and the rope holds its shape under load, so a Distel or VT grabs and releases predictably and a mechanical device does not flatten the line into an oval after a season of use.

On a stationary rope the low stretch means less bounce when you start a pitch, and on a moving rope it feeds through a friction saver without a lot of drag. Compare it with other 16-strand climbing ropes if you want a softer or lighter hand.

Check the manufacturer's compatibility list before pairing tygra with a specific device, and match your hitch cord to the rope diameter. Keep it in a rope bag, out of bar oil and fuel, and away from sharp edges and running saws.

Treat it as life-support gear: follow the manufacturer's instructions, check it before every climb, and retire it after a hard fall, a drop onto a hard surface, or any damage you can't explain. Use it within an ANSI Z133 program and only after proper training. Retire the rope if you find glazing, cuts through the cover, core damage or stiff spots.

faq.q: Can I use tygra for SRS?
faq.a: Yes. It is designed for both moving-rope and stationary-rope climbing. Confirm your specific device is approved for it in the device maker's instructions.

faq.q: Is tygra good for rigging?
faq.a: No. Keep climbing rope for life support only and use a dedicated rigging line for lowering wood.

name: Yale Phantom Lanyard (Pink and Black, No Hardware)
title: Yale Phantom Lanyard, Pink and Black (No Hardware)
h1: Yale Phantom Pink and Black Lanyard Without Hardware
meta: The Yale Phantom lanyard in pink and black, sold without hardware so you can set it up with your own adjuster and carabiners. Setup tips and inspection notes.
tagline: A pink and black rope lanyard sold bare so you can build it your way.
summary: The Yale Phantom lanyard comes without hardware, so you pick the adjuster, snap or carabiners that fit your climbing style. The pink and black color makes it easy to tell apart from your climbing line and the rest of the crew's gear.
highlights: Sold without hardware for a custom setup
High-visibility pink and black colorway
Pairs with a mechanical adjuster or a friction hitch
Rope lanyard for positioning on the stem

p: Buying a lanyard without hardware makes sense if you already own a favorite adjuster or want to match the carabiners on the rest of your saddle. Most climbers run it with a mechanical adjuster or a hitch on one end and a locking connector on both ends, set up as a 2-in-1 or a standard flipline.

Bright, two-tone rope also helps the ground crew. They can see at a glance which line is your lanyard when they are watching you work, and you are less likely to grab the wrong tail when you are tired. Mark the date you put it in service on a tag or in your gear log so you know how old it is when inspection time comes.

Match any adjuster to the rope diameter listed by its maker, and check that the eye fits your carabiner without side-loading the gate. See our fliplines and lanyards for complete kits if you would rather buy it ready to climb.

A lanyard is your second point of attachment when you cut, so keep it snug and above the saw's path. Never cut toward your lanyard, and choose a steel-core flipline when you are removing wood close to it with a saw.

Treat it as life-support gear: follow the manufacturer's instructions, check it before every climb, and retire it after a hard fall, a drop onto a hard surface, or any damage you can't explain. Use it within an ANSI Z133 program and only after proper training.

faq.q: What hardware does it need?
faq.a: At minimum a locking carabiner or snap at each end and an adjuster or friction hitch. Use hardware rated for life support and compatible with the rope diameter.

faq.q: Is this lanyard cut resistant?
faq.a: It is a rope lanyard, not a wire-core flipline. Keep the saw well away from it.

name: HAIX Protector Ultra Chainsaw Boots
title: HAIX Protector Ultra Chainsaw Boots
meta: HAIX Protector Ultra chainsaw boots are leather saw boots for ground crews and fellers. What the protection covers, fit tips and how to keep them in shape.
tagline: Leather chainsaw-protective boots for fellers and ground crew on the saw all day.
summary: The HAIX Protector Ultra is a leather chainsaw boot made for crews who run a saw on the ground every day. It combines cut-protective inserts with a supportive, laced fit for felling, bucking and brush work on rough ground.
highlights: Chainsaw-protective boot for ground saw work
Leather upper with a supportive laced fit
Aggressive sole for slopes, logs and wet ground
Built for long days on the saw

p: Chaps and saw pants stop most cuts above the ankle, but a kickback or a slip while bucking can put the chain on your foot. A chainsaw-protective boot adds fibers in the upper that clog the sprocket, plus a protective toe, so your feet get the same kind of protection your legs do.

Saw boots also need to work with the rest of your kit. Check that your chaps or saw pants overlap the top of the boot with no gap when you kneel, and that the sole has the grip you need on wet bark and steep ground. A boot that fits well is one you will actually wear on the hot afternoons, which is when most people cut corners.
The Protector Ultra is built for ground crews who stand on logs, brush piles and side hills. Browse our arborist boots if you also need a lighter climbing boot.

Try boots on in the afternoon with the socks you wear at work, and give them a week of short days to break in. Clean off mud and sap, dry them away from direct heat, and treat the leather so it stays supple.
Check the protection rating on the boot label against what your employer or the job requires. No boot is cut-proof, so keep good saw technique, a sharp chain and a working chain brake.

faq.q: Are these good for climbing?
faq.a: They are a heavier ground and felling boot. Many climbers prefer a lighter boot for spurs or SRS and keep saw boots for ground days.

faq.q: Do I still need chaps or saw pants?
faq.a: Yes. Boots protect the feet; leg protection is still required for chainsaw work on the ground.

name: DMM Ceros Locksafe Carabiner with Captive Bar
title: DMM Ceros Locksafe Carabiner with Captive Bar
h1: DMM Ceros Locksafe Carabiner with Captive Bar
meta: The DMM Ceros Locksafe carabiner has a captive bar that holds a load in place and stops cross-loading. Where arborists use it and how to check it before use.
tagline: An auto-locking carabiner with a captive bar that keeps the load where it belongs.
summary: The DMM Ceros carabiner pairs a Locksafe auto-locking gate with a captive bar that holds a device or rope in one position. That keeps the load off the minor axis, which is useful anywhere a connector could rotate on a bridge, ring or device.
highlights: Captive bar holds the load in position
Locksafe auto-locking gate
Helps prevent cross-loading
Useful for devices, bridges and fixed attachments

p: A carabiner that can rotate can end up loaded across the gate, where it is much weaker. The Ceros bar splits the basket so a device, eye or ring stays at the spine end. Climbers use it to attach a mechanical device to a bridge, to hold a rope wrench tether in line, or anywhere they want the connector to stay oriented.

Keep the Ceros dedicated to the job you set it up for. Moving it between roles makes it easy to forget which side of the bar carries the load. Many climbers mark it with colored tape on the spine, away from the gate and the rope-bearing surfaces, so it stays on the device it belongs to.
The Locksafe gate needs a deliberate sequence to open, so it will not roll open against bark or a branch. See our other auto-locking carabiners for different shapes and sizes.

Open and close the gate and make sure it snaps fully shut and locks on its own. Look for grooves worn by rope, burrs, cracks or a sticky gate, and clean out grit with warm water if the action slows down.

Treat it as life-support gear: follow the manufacturer's instructions, check it before every climb, and retire it after a hard fall, a drop onto a hard surface, or any damage you can't explain. Use it within an ANSI Z133 program and only after proper training.

faq.q: Does the bar reduce strength?
faq.a: The rated strengths are marked on the spine. Load it along the major axis as shown in DMM's instructions.

faq.q: Can I clip a rope through the bar side?
faq.a: Follow DMM's diagrams for which side to load. The bar is meant to keep the load in the spine-side section.

name: DMM Shadow HMS Locksafe Carabiner (Matt Gray)
title: DMM Shadow HMS Carabiner, Matt Gray
meta: The DMM Shadow HMS carabiner in matt gray: a pear-shaped auto-locker with a wide basket for hitches and rope. Arborist uses, sizing notes and inspection tips.
tagline: A pear-shaped HMS auto-locker with room for a hitch, a rope and a bit of hardware.
summary: The DMM Shadow HMS carabiner is a pear-shaped locking connector with a wide, rounded basket. The matt gray finish keeps glare down and the HMS shape gives a hitch or rope room to sit flat.
highlights: Pear (HMS) shape with a wide basket
Auto-locking gate
Matt gray finish
Good for hitches, bridges and anchors

body.h: Where an HMS fits on a saddle
p: The wide end of an HMS gives a friction hitch, a Munter or two ropes space to lie flat instead of pinching. Arborists use the Shadow to tie into a bridge, to connect a hitch and pulley, or as a general anchor carabiner when building a canopy anchor or a basal setup.

The wide nose also makes it easier to clip and unclip with gloves on, which helps on cold mornings. If you carry several lockers, a different finish makes it quick to pick out the one you use for your hitch or anchor without looking twice.
Because the basket is generous, it also handles thicker rope and stacked hardware better than a small D. Compare sizes in our auto-locking carabiners.

Check that the gate closes and locks by itself every time, and watch for rope wear grooves at the basket, which form faster when rope runs over the carabiner. Rinse grit out with clean water and let it dry before storage.

Treat it as life-support gear: follow the manufacturer's instructions, check it before every climb, and retire it after a hard fall, a drop onto a hard surface, or any damage you can't explain. Use it within an ANSI Z133 program and only after proper training.

faq.q: What does HMS mean?
faq.a: It refers to the pear shape designed for a Munter hitch. The wide end gives rope and hitches more room.

faq.q: Is the matt finish just cosmetic?
faq.a: Mostly. It reduces shine and helps you tell this carabiner apart from others on your saddle.

name: DMM Zodiac Locking Carabiner (Matt Gray)
title: DMM Zodiac Carabiner, Matt Gray
meta: The DMM Zodiac carabiner in matt gray is a locking connector for climbing systems. Where it fits on a tree climbing setup, what to check and how to care for it.
tagline: A locking DMM carabiner in matt gray for everyday climbing connections.
summary: The DMM Zodiac carabiner is a locking aluminum connector in a low-glare matt gray finish. It is a practical choice for routine connections on a climbing system, such as hitch-to-bridge or lanyard ends.
highlights: Locking gate for life-support connections
Matt gray finish cuts glare
Light aluminum body
Fits everyday saddle and hitch connections

body.h: Using the Zodiac in a climbing system
p: A tree climber's saddle can carry half a dozen locking connectors, each doing a slightly different job. The Zodiac is a general-purpose locker: clip it to a lanyard eye, use it between a hitch and your bridge, or keep it as a spare for building anchors.

Before you buy, think about what the Zodiac will carry. A rope eye, a micro pulley and a hitch cord all take space in the basket, and a connector that is too small will crowd the gate and pinch the hitch. Lay your gear out and clip it together on the ground to check the fit before you commit it to your climbing system.
Check the strength markings on the spine and confirm the gate type before you assign it to a life-support role. You can compare shapes and gate styles in our auto-locking carabiners.
Load carabiners along the spine and avoid three-way loading or loading across the gate. Keep them out of fuel and bar oil, which collect grit and slow the gate.

Treat it as life-support gear: follow the manufacturer's instructions, check it before every climb, and retire it after a hard fall, a drop onto a hard surface, or any damage you can't explain. Use it within an ANSI Z133 program and only after proper training.

faq.q: Does it lock automatically?
faq.a: It is listed with our auto-locking carabiners. Check the gate on the exact version you buy, since some DMM models come in more than one gate style.

faq.q: Is it rated for arborist climbing?
faq.a: Check the markings on the spine and DMM's instructions against your employer's requirements under ANSI Z133.

name: ISC Offset D Supersafe Carabiner
title: ISC Offset D Supersafe Carabiner
meta: The ISC Offset D Supersafe carabiner is an offset D auto-locker for tree climbing systems. How the shape helps, where to clip it, and what to check before use.
tagline: An offset D auto-locker from ISC for strong, tidy connections on your saddle.
summary: The ISC Offset D Supersafe carabiner combines an offset D shape with ISC's auto-locking Supersafe gate. The offset D keeps the load near the spine while opening wide enough to clip rope eyes, rings and devices.
highlights: Offset D shape keeps loads near the spine
Supersafe auto-locking gate
Wide gate opening for eyes and rings
Made by ISC, a UK rigging and climbing maker

p: An offset D puts the load close to the spine, which is the strongest part of a carabiner, while the wider gate end makes clipping a thick eye splice or a pulley side plate easier. That makes it a good all-rounder for hitch climbing systems, lanyard ends and connecting to a bridge.

Look at how the gate sits on your saddle when you build your system. An offset D clipped to a bridge or lanyard ring should hang with the gate facing out and away from bark, so it does not get pushed open against a stem. Set it up on the ground, hang in it, and check the orientation before you leave the ground.
The Supersafe gate is designed so it cannot be opened by a single accidental motion. See other auto-locking carabiners if you prefer an oval or HMS shape.
Make sure the gate closes fully and the lock engages without help. Look for cracks, deep rope grooves and corrosion, especially if you work near salt air or treated wood.

Treat it as life-support gear: follow the manufacturer's instructions, check it before every climb, and retire it after a hard fall, a drop onto a hard surface, or any damage you can't explain. Use it within an ANSI Z133 program and only after proper training.

faq.q: Is the Supersafe gate triple action?
faq.a: It is ISC's auto-locking gate design that needs more than one deliberate motion to open. Check ISC's instructions for the exact opening sequence.

faq.q: Steel or aluminum?
faq.a: ISC makes offset D carabiners in more than one material. Check the listing and the spine markings for the version you buy.

name: KONG Ovalone Aluminum Auto-Locking Carabiner
title: KONG Ovalone Aluminum Auto-Locking Carabiner
meta: The KONG Ovalone aluminum auto-locking carabiner is a symmetric oval for pulleys, devices and racking. Where an oval shines on a climbing rig and what to check.
tagline: A symmetric aluminum oval that keeps pulleys and devices centered.
summary: The KONG Ovalone aluminum auto-locking carabiner is a classic symmetric oval. Its even shape lets pulleys, rope grabs and other hardware sit centered, which is why ovals stay popular for rescue kits, rigging setups and climbing systems.
highlights: Symmetric oval shape centers hardware
Auto-locking gate
Lighter aluminum version of a classic design
Works well with pulleys and devices

body.h: Where an oval earns its spot
p: An oval loads evenly on both sides, so a pulley or device does not shift toward the gate. That makes the Ovalone a natural match for haul systems, mechanical advantage setups, rope grabs and racking several pieces of hardware together.

On the ground, an oval is also handy for racking. Clip pulleys, rope grabs and spare connectors to one carabiner on a gear loop and they stay organized and easy to grab when the climber calls for something. Keep life-support connectors on a separate, clearly marked rack so they do not get mixed with rigging hardware.
Ovals are not as strong as D shapes of similar weight, so check the spine markings and match the carabiner to the job. Compare it with our other auto-locking carabiners.

Keep the gate clean and lubricate it sparingly with a product the manufacturer approves if it starts to drag. Look for wear grooves where rope runs and replace the carabiner if the gate fails to close by itself.

Treat it as life-support gear: follow the manufacturer's instructions, check it before every climb, and retire it after a hard fall, a drop onto a hard surface, or any damage you can't explain. Use it within an ANSI Z133 program and only after proper training.

faq.q: Is an oval good for my climbing hitch?
faq.a: It can work, but many climbers prefer an HMS or offset D for hitches. Ovals shine with pulleys and devices.

faq.q: Is there a steel version?
faq.a: KONG also makes the Ovalone in steel. Choose steel for heavy wear and aluminum to save weight.

name: Knots at Work: A Field Guide for the Modern Arborist
title: Knots at Work: A Field Guide for the Modern Arborist
h1: Knots at Work: A Field Guide for the Modern Arborist
meta: Knots at Work is a field guide to the knots and hitches arborists use for climbing and rigging. Who it suits, how to study it, and why practice still matters.
tagline: A pocket field guide to the knots and hitches tree workers use every day.
summary: Knots at Work: A Field Guide for the Modern Arborist covers the knots and hitches tree workers tie for climbing, rigging and everyday ground work. It is a handy reference for new climbers and a refresher for crew leaders training others.
highlights: Knots and hitches for climbing and rigging
Field guide format for use on the job
Useful for training new ground workers and climbers
Good reference for crew leaders

p: Every tree job runs on a short list of knots: a bowline or running bowline for rigging, a clove hitch and half hitches for tying off, stopper knots, and friction hitches for climbing. A field guide puts them in one place so a new hire can study on the ride to the job and a crew leader can check a detail before teaching it.

A good way to use it is to pick one knot a week, tie it on every job, and talk through when it is the right choice. Ground workers who know their knots make rigging safer and faster, because the climber can call for a hitch and trust that it will be tied and dressed correctly. Keep the guide in the truck where the crew can find it.
Pair it with hands-on practice and the rest of our books and training materials for a fuller picture of climbing and rigging.

Tie each knot until you can dress and set it with your eyes closed, then have an experienced climber check it. A knot that looks right in a picture can still be tied wrong, and a poorly dressed hitch can slip.
A book is no substitute for training. Learn life-support knots under supervision, follow ANSI Z133 and your employer's procedures, and always check your system before you leave the ground.

faq.q: Is this for beginners?
faq.a: Yes. It suits new climbers and ground workers, and it is a handy refresher for experienced crew members.

faq.q: Can I learn to climb from it?
faq.a: No. Use it alongside hands-on training from a qualified climber or training provider.

name: AE2129 Bucket Scuff Pad
title: AE2129 Scuff Pad for Bucket Trucks
meta: The AE2129 scuff pad protects an aerial lift bucket from rubbing and wear. What a bucket truck scuff pad does, how to fit it, and how to keep the bucket clean.
tagline: A replacement scuff pad that protects an aerial lift bucket from wear.
summary: The AE2129 is a bucket truck scuff pad that takes the rubbing and abrasion that would otherwise wear down an aerial lift bucket. It is a simple part that helps keep the bucket in good shape on busy trimming crews.
highlights: Protects the bucket from rubbing and wear
Replacement part for aerial lift trucks
Helps keep the bucket surface in good condition
Simple maintenance item for line-clearance crews

p: A bucket gets dragged against limbs, pole hardware and the truck body all day. A scuff pad takes that wear in place of the bucket shell, and it is far cheaper to replace than repairing a damaged bucket. Crews also fit pads where tools and saws rest so they do not grind into the bucket.

Scuff pads are a wear item, so it pays to keep a spare on the truck. When you swap one, clean the mounting area, check the fasteners and look for any cracks or gouges in the bucket underneath. Catching wear early is cheaper than replacing a bucket or liner, and it keeps the truck ready for the next job.
Check the part number against your bucket and truck model before ordering. You can find liners, covers and other bucket truck accessories in the same section.

On insulated aerial devices, anything that cuts or gouges the bucket or liner can matter for dielectric protection. Inspect the bucket and liner on your daily walk-around, keep them clean of sap and debris, and follow the truck manufacturer's guidance for any added parts.
Wear the fall protection your employer and the lift maker require whenever you are in the bucket, and keep minimum approach distances to energized lines under ANSI Z133.

faq.q: Will it fit my bucket?
faq.a: Match the AE2129 part number to your equipment or ask the truck or bucket supplier before ordering.

faq.q: Does it change the bucket's insulation rating?
faq.a: Follow the lift and bucket maker's instructions for any attachments, and have insulated equipment tested on schedule.

name: Chainsaw Strap with Snap
title: Chainsaw Strap with Snap for Climbing Saws
meta: A chainsaw strap with a snap keeps your climbing saw tethered to your saddle so it can't fall. How to set it up, where to clip it, and what to check each day.
tagline: A simple saw strap with a snap to keep your climbing saw tethered aloft.
summary: This chainsaw strap with snap tethers your saw to your saddle, so a dropped saw hangs from your hip instead of falling into the drop zone. It is one of the simplest pieces of gear on a climber's harness and one of the most useful.
highlights: Keeps a climbing saw tethered to the saddle
Snap for quick connection to the saw ring
Protects the ground crew from a dropped saw
Simple, low-cost tool tether

p: Clip the snap to the lanyard ring on your saw and attach the other end to a saw ring or D on your saddle. The strap lets you hang the saw out of the way while you reposition, and if it slips out of your hand it stays with you instead of landing on someone below.

Keep the strap long enough that you can make a full cut without the saw being held back, but short enough that the saw cannot swing down to your knees or tangle with your lanyard. Check the length after you change saddles or saws, because a small difference in where the ring sits changes how the saw hangs.
Set the length so the saw hangs clear of your legs and your lanyard. Browse our chainsaw lanyards for bungee and adjustable versions.
A saw strap is a tool tether, not life-support gear. Never clip into it for positioning or use it as a lanyard.

Check the strap for cuts and the snap for a sticky or bent gate before each climb, and replace it when it is worn. Keep the saw's chain brake on when it is hanging and clear the area below before you work.

faq.q: Can I use this as a lanyard?
faq.a: No. It is only for tethering the saw. Use a rated lanyard and carabiners for positioning.

faq.q: Where do I clip it on my saddle?
faq.a: Most climbers clip to a dedicated saw ring or tool loop on the side opposite their lanyard.

name: Ring-to-Ring Basic Chainsaw Lanyard
title: Ring-to-Ring Basic Chainsaw Lanyard
meta: A ring-to-ring basic chainsaw lanyard tethers a climbing saw to your saddle. How the ring ends work, how to set the length, and why it is never life support.
tagline: A basic chainsaw lanyard with a ring at each end for a clean saw tether.
summary: This ring-to-ring basic chainsaw lanyard links your saw to your saddle with a ring on each end. It is a simple, sturdy way to keep a top-handle saw attached while you climb, cut and reposition.
highlights: Ring at each end for easy connection
Keeps the saw tethered while climbing
Basic, durable design
Pairs with a snap or small carabiner

p: Rings at both ends let you choose how you attach. Many climbers girth or clip one ring to the saw's lanyard point and clip the other to their saddle with a snap or small carabiner. A tethered saw can hang out of the way while you move, and it stays with you if it gets knocked loose.

A basic ring-to-ring lanyard is also easy to replace when it wears out, and it is cheap enough to keep a spare in the truck. If you climb with more than one saw, give each saw its own lanyard so you are not unclipping and moving hardware in the tree.
Pick a length that lets you cut comfortably without the saw swinging into your legs or your climbing line. See all chainsaw lanyards for stretch and adjustable styles.
This lanyard is for the saw only. Never use it for positioning, fall protection or rigging.

Check the webbing or cord and the stitching before each climb and replace it if it is cut, frayed or glazed. Engage the chain brake before letting the saw hang, and keep the ground crew out of the drop zone while you work.

faq.q: What do I connect the rings with?
faq.a: A snap or small carabiner on the saddle side is common. It does not need to be life-support rated since it carries the saw only.

faq.q: Will it fit my top-handle saw?
faq.a: It fits saws with a lanyard ring or attachment point, which most top-handle saws have.

name: Clogger TreeCrew Men's Chainsaw Pants
title: Clogger TreeCrew Men's Chainsaw Pants
meta: Clogger TreeCrew men's chainsaw pants give climbers and ground crew cut protection with a lighter, cooler feel. Fit tips, care and what the pants cover.
tagline: Light, breathable chainsaw pants built for climbers and busy ground crews.
summary: Clogger TreeCrew men's chainsaw pants put cut protection into a lighter, more breathable pant than traditional chaps. They are built for arborists who climb, drag brush and run a saw in the same day and want to stay cool doing it.
highlights: Chainsaw cut protection built into the pant
Lighter and more breathable than many saw pants
Designed for climbing and ground work
Fitted cut that moves with you

p: Chaps go on and off fast, but they can twist, snag and trap heat. Saw pants keep the protection where it belongs whether you are kneeling to buck, climbing a spar or walking brush to the chipper. Clogger built the TreeCrew line around comfort, so they are a common pick for crews in hot weather.

Fit matters with saw pants. Try them on with your saddle and climbing gear, kneel and step up as if you were climbing, and make sure the protective panels stay in front of your legs. Pants that are too long can catch on spurs, and pants that are too tight wear quickly at the seat and knees.
Check the protection class and coverage on the label against your job's requirements. Compare options in our chainsaw pants section.
Wash saw pants as the label directs; the wrong detergent, bleach or heat can damage the protective fibers. Patch only the outer fabric with methods Clogger approves.

Retire the pants after any cut that reaches the protective layer, since those fibers have done their job and will not stop another cut. Saw pants reduce injury; they do not replace a sharp chain, a working chain brake and good technique.

faq.q: Can I wear these while climbing?
faq.a: Yes. They are made for climbers as well as ground crews, with a fit that moves with you.

faq.q: Can I repair a cut?
faq.a: Not in the protective layer. If a cut reaches the inner fibers, replace the pants.

name: KONG Indy Evo Plus Descender
title: KONG Indy Evo Plus Descender
meta: The KONG Indy Evo Plus is a self-braking descender for controlled descents and rope work. What it does, where it fits for tree workers, and training notes.
tagline: A self-braking rope descender for controlled lowering and rope access work.
summary: The KONG Indy Evo Plus descender is a self-braking device for controlled descents on a single rope. Tree workers and rope access crews use this type of descender for rescue kits, access lines and stationary-rope work where a handled descender makes sense.
highlights: Self-braking descender design
Handle for controlled descent
Suited to rope access and rescue kits
Made by KONG in Italy

body.h: Where it fits for tree work
p: Most climbing arborists use a dedicated SRS device, but a handled self-braking descender has a place in aerial rescue kits, for accessing a tree on a fixed line, and on crews that also do rope access work. The handle lets you control speed, and the device is designed to hold when you let go.

If you are thinking of adding a descender like this to your kit, start by working out what role it will play: rescue, access or regular descent. Each role sets different needs for rope type, backup and anchor, and those choices shape the rest of your system. Talk it through with an experienced climber or trainer first.
Check the rope diameter range and approved rope types in KONG's instructions before setting it up. See our ascent and descent gear for arborist-specific devices.
Descenders behave differently on different ropes, wet or dry. Practice close to the ground first and always use a backup or stopper knot as the manufacturer directs.

Treat it as life-support gear: follow the manufacturer's instructions, check it before every climb, and retire it after a hard fall, a drop onto a hard surface, or any damage you can't explain. Use it within an ANSI Z133 program and only after proper training.

faq.q: Can I use it for SRS tree climbing?
faq.a: It is built for descent and rope access. Check KONG's instructions for approved uses before including it in a tree climbing system.

faq.q: What rope does it take?
faq.a: Use the rope diameters and types listed in KONG's instructions for your exact version.

name: Petzl PANTIN Foot Ascender
title: Petzl PANTIN Foot Ascender for SRS Climbing
meta: The Petzl PANTIN foot ascender helps you walk up a stationary rope on SRS. How it fits a climbing system, left and right versions, and what to check before use.
tagline: A foot ascender that lets your legs do the work on a stationary rope.
summary: The Petzl PANTIN foot ascender straps to your boot and grabs the rope as you step, so you can walk up a stationary rope. Paired with a chest or knee ascender, it makes SRS ascents faster and less tiring.
highlights: Straps to the boot for rope walking
Speeds up SRS ascents
Available in left and right foot versions
Pairs with a chest or knee ascender system

body.h: How it speeds up an ascent
p: On a stationary rope, the PANTIN grips the line each time you step down and slides up as you lift your foot. Combined with a chest ascender or a knee system, you can walk up long access lines without burning out your arms, then switch to your descent device at the top.

Setting up a rope walking system takes some fine tuning. The foot ascender should sit snugly on your boot, and your chest or knee ascender should be adjusted so the rope runs straight between them. Spend time at ground level getting the setup right before you start long ascents.
Climbers usually run it on the right or left foot to match their other ascenders. Browse our foot ascenders and foot loops for alternatives.
The PANTIN is an aid to climbing, not a primary attachment point. Always stay connected to the rope with your main ascent system or device.

Check the cam teeth, spring and strap before each climb, and keep mud and sap out of the cam. Follow Petzl's instructions, learn rope walking under supervision, and work within your crew's ANSI Z133 procedures.

faq.q: Is the PANTIN life-support gear?
faq.a: No. It assists ascent. Your main connection to the rope must be through a rated device or ascender system.

faq.q: Left or right?
faq.a: Choose the foot you want to lead with. Some climbers run one on each foot.

name: Weaver Foot Loop Ascender
title: Weaver Foot Loop Ascender
meta: The Weaver foot loop ascender adds a foot loop to your climbing system so your legs help on the way up. Setup tips, sizing, and what to inspect before you climb.
tagline: A foot loop that lets your legs help on the climb up the rope.
summary: The Weaver foot loop ascender gives you a foot loop to push against while ascending, so your legs do more of the lifting. It is a simple add-on for climbers who want an easier ascent on a doubled or single rope.
highlights: Foot loop for leg-powered ascent
Pairs with a hand ascender or hitch system
Simple setup
Made by Weaver, a long-time arborist gear maker

body.h: How climbers use a foot loop
p: A foot loop attached to a hand ascender lets you stand up in the loop, then slide your hitch or tend your system as you rise. It turns a hand-over-hand climb into a stand-and-sit rhythm that is much easier on the arms, especially on long first pitches.

A foot loop also helps with getting back on the rope after a rest or a repositioning, and it makes it easier to stand up and reach a high branch union. Keep it short enough that you can step into it without swinging your leg out wide.
Adjust the loop so you can stand comfortably with the ascender at about head height. See our foot ascenders and foot loops for other options.
A foot loop is an aid, not a life-support connection. Stay tied in to your primary climbing system at all times.
Inspect the loop and stitching before each climb and replace it if worn or cut. Learn your ascent system low and slow with an experienced climber, and follow your crew's procedures under ANSI Z133.

faq.q: Does it include a hand ascender?
faq.a: Check the listing. Foot loops are often sold on their own to pair with an ascender you already own.

faq.q: Can I use it on SRS and MRS?
faq.a: Foot loops are used with both. The rest of your system must be set up correctly for the technique.

name: Climbing Technology Quick Roll Hand Ascender
title: CT Quick Roll Hand Ascender with Pulley
meta: The CT Quick Roll is a handled ascender with a built-in pulley for ascents and haul systems. How tree workers use it, setup notes and inspection before climbing.
tagline: A handled ascender with a built-in pulley for climbing and hauling.
summary: The CT Quick Roll hand ascender pairs a handled rope clamp with a built-in pulley. That makes it useful both for ascending a stationary rope and for building a quick progress-capture haul system.
highlights: Handled ascender with integrated pulley
Works for ascent and haul systems
Comfortable grip for long pitches
Made by Climbing Technology in Italy

p: As a hand ascender, the Quick Roll grips a stationary line while you stand in a foot loop or push off a foot ascender. Because the pulley sits right below the cam, you can also run a rope back through it to build a simple haul or tensioning system without adding a separate pulley.

It can also help on the ground when you need to tension a line or haul a rope bag up to a climber. Using one tool for both jobs saves weight on your saddle, but make sure every use fits within the loads and roles the manufacturer lists. Keep climbing gear and rigging gear separate when you can.
Check the rope diameter range and approved uses in Climbing Technology's instructions. See our ascent and descent gear for devices that work with it.
A hand ascender is part of a system. Never rely on it alone; stay connected with your primary device and a backup as instructed.

Treat it as life-support gear: follow the manufacturer's instructions, check it before every climb, and retire it after a hard fall, a drop onto a hard surface, or any damage you can't explain. Use it within an ANSI Z133 program and only after proper training.

faq.q: Can I use it for rigging?
faq.a: Use it only within the loads and uses CT lists. For tree rigging, use dedicated rigging gear.

faq.q: Is there a left-hand version?
faq.a: Many handled ascenders come in left and right versions. Check the listing for the hand you need.

name: Replacement Parts for SpiderJack 2:1
title: SpiderJack 2:1 Replacement Parts
meta: Replacement parts for the ART SpiderJack 2:1 mechanical climbing device. What to replace, how to match parts to your version, and when to retire the device.
tagline: Genuine service parts to keep a SpiderJack climbing device running right.
summary: These replacement parts for the SpiderJack 2:1 let you service worn components on ART's mechanical MRS climbing device. Using the right parts keeps the device working the way it was designed instead of retiring it early.
highlights: Service parts for the SpiderJack 2:1
Keeps a mechanical MRS device in working order
Match parts to your device version
Follow ART's service instructions

p: A mechanical friction device takes rope wear, grit and sap every climb. Parts such as springs, pins and wear components eventually need replacing, and fitting them is far cheaper than a new device. Confirm which parts are in the kit and that they match your SpiderJack version before you order.

Keep the old parts until the device has been tested with the new ones, in case you need to compare them. Write down the date and what you replaced in your gear log, so you know the service history the next time you inspect the device or hand it to another climber.
If you are shopping for a complete device, see our MRS climbing devices.
Only replace parts that ART allows users to replace, and follow its service instructions exactly. If a part requires factory service, send the device back rather than improvising a repair.

After any service, function-test the device low to the ground before climbing. Retire it if you see cracks, deformation or wear beyond ART's limits, and keep a record of inspections as part of your ANSI Z133 program.

faq.q: Will these fit a SpiderJack 3?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Match parts to the exact model and version you own.

faq.q: Can I service it myself?
faq.a: Only for parts ART lists as user-replaceable. Otherwise use manufacturer service.

name: Rock Exotica RockGrab 90
title: Rock Exotica RockGrab 90 Rope Grab
meta: The Rock Exotica RockGrab 90 is a rope grab for backup and progress capture on fixed lines. How tree crews use rope grabs, setup notes and inspection steps.
tagline: A rope grab for backup and progress capture on a fixed line.
summary: The Rock Exotica RockGrab 90 is a rope grab that rides a fixed line and locks when loaded. Crews use rope grabs as a backup on access lines and to capture progress in haul and tensioning systems.
highlights: Rope grab for fixed lines
Locks quickly when loaded
Useful as a backup or progress capture
Made in the USA by Rock Exotica

p: A rope grab follows you along a line and locks if you load it suddenly, which makes it a common backup on access and rope work. On the rigging side, it can serve as a progress capture so a haul system holds its gains when you reset.

Rope grabs work best on the rope types they were designed for. Wet, icy or muddy rope can change how quickly the cam bites, so check how it behaves in the conditions you will be working in. Keep the rope above the grab clear of edges that could cut it when loaded.
Match the device to the rope diameter and type in Rock Exotica's instructions. Compare it with other rope grabs before you choose.
Install a rope grab the right way up; a reversed grab will not lock. Test it on the rope at ground level before every use.

Treat it as life-support gear: follow the manufacturer's instructions, check it before every climb, and retire it after a hard fall, a drop onto a hard surface, or any damage you can't explain. Use it within an ANSI Z133 program and only after proper training.

faq.q: Is it a fall arrest device?
faq.a: Use it only in the roles Rock Exotica lists for it, and only as part of a properly designed system.

faq.q: What rope does it fit?
faq.a: Check Rock Exotica's instructions for the approved diameter range and rope types.

name: DMM Boa Locksafe Carabiner
title: DMM Boa Locksafe Gate Carabiner
meta: The DMM Boa Locksafe is a large D carabiner with an auto-locking gate for anchors and multiple connections. Where it fits on a tree rig and what to inspect.
tagline: A big D-shaped auto-locker with room for anchors and multiple connections.
summary: The DMM Boa Locksafe gate carabiner is a large D-shaped connector with DMM's auto-locking Locksafe gate. Its roomy basket makes it a good anchor or master carabiner when you need to clip several things at once.
highlights: Large D shape with a roomy basket
Locksafe auto-locking gate
Good for anchors and multiple connections
Load stays close to the strong spine

body.h: When you need a bigger carabiner
p: A small connector fills up fast once you add a sling, a pulley and a rope eye. The Boa gives you space to clip several items without crowding the gate. Arborists use it as a master carabiner on an anchor, for connecting thick slings, or anywhere a standard D feels tight.

The Boa also makes a good choice when you want one carabiner to collect several anchor legs or slings at a single point. Keep the connections tidy so nothing crosses over the gate, and check the whole anchor before you load it.
The Locksafe gate opens with a deliberate motion and locks on its own when released. Compare it with our other auto-locking carabiners.
Even a big carabiner should be loaded along its spine. Avoid three-way loading and keep loads off the gate.

Treat it as life-support gear: follow the manufacturer's instructions, check it before every climb, and retire it after a hard fall, a drop onto a hard surface, or any damage you can't explain. Use it within an ANSI Z133 program and only after proper training.

faq.q: Is the Boa good for climbing?
faq.a: It works on climbing systems, but its size makes it best for anchors and multiple connections rather than a small hitch.

faq.q: Steel or aluminum?
faq.a: Check the listing and spine markings for the version you buy.

name: DMM Klettersteig ANSI Gate-Rated Carabiner
title: DMM Klettersteig ANSI Gate-Rated Carabiner
meta: The DMM Klettersteig ANSI gate-rated carabiner is a large-opening auto-locker with a strong gate. Where it fits on a tree climbing setup and what to check.
tagline: A large-opening auto-locker with an ANSI gate rating for demanding connections.
summary: The DMM Klettersteig ANSI gate-rated carabiner combines a wide gate opening with a gate strength rated to ANSI requirements. That makes it a good fit where a carabiner might be loaded against the gate or needs to clip large anchors and lanyard rings.
highlights: ANSI gate-rated version
Large gate opening
Auto-locking gate
Good for lanyards, anchors and large connections

p: Arborists sometimes work in places where a carabiner can roll against a limb or a ring. A gate rated to ANSI requirements gives extra margin in those cases. The large opening also makes it easy to clip around a wide lanyard ring, a big eye splice or an anchor sling.

Because it is large, the Klettersteig is not the best pick for every job on your saddle. Use it where the size and gate strength matter, such as lanyard ends or anchors, and use smaller connectors for hitches and devices where weight and space are tight.
Check the strengths stamped on the spine and gate to confirm it meets your employer's requirements. Compare it with our other auto-locking carabiners.
Open and release the gate several times to make sure it closes and locks on its own. Look for cracks, grooves, burrs or corrosion and keep it clean of grit and sap.

Treat it as life-support gear: follow the manufacturer's instructions, check it before every climb, and retire it after a hard fall, a drop onto a hard surface, or any damage you can't explain. Use it within an ANSI Z133 program and only after proper training.

faq.q: What is ANSI gate rating?
faq.a: It means the gate is rated to an ANSI fall protection requirement for gate strength. Check the markings for the exact standard and values.

faq.q: Is it too big for a saddle?
faq.a: It is larger than a typical hitch carabiner, so many climbers use it on lanyards or anchors.

name: DMM Revolver Locking Carabiner
title: DMM Revolver Carabiner with Built-In Pulley
meta: The DMM Revolver carabiner has a built-in pulley wheel that cuts rope friction. How tree climbers use it for redirects and mechanical advantage, plus care tips.
tagline: A carabiner with a built-in pulley wheel to cut friction on redirects.
summary: The DMM Revolver carabiner has a small pulley wheel built into its basket, so rope runs over a rolling sheave instead of bare metal. That cuts friction on redirects, hauling lines and simple mechanical advantage setups.
highlights: Built-in pulley wheel in the basket
Reduces rope friction and wear
Locking version
Useful for redirects and haul systems

p: Every time rope bends over a carabiner it loses energy to friction. The Revolver's wheel lets the rope roll instead, which makes a difference on redirects, hauling a rope or tool up to a climber, or building a quick 3:1 to tension a line. Climbers also use it to tend slack on a hitch system.

Climbers who use the Revolver often clip it to a bridge or a point on their saddle so they can pull slack through quickly as they climb. It is also a handy redirect on a long limb walk, where reducing friction makes it easier to keep tension on your system.
The wheel is small, so it is a friction reducer, not a full-size rigging pulley. See our other auto-locking carabiners for standard shapes.
Check that the wheel spins freely and that the gate closes and locks. Rinse out grit and sap, which can jam the wheel.

Treat it as life-support gear: follow the manufacturer's instructions, check it before every climb, and retire it after a hard fall, a drop onto a hard surface, or any damage you can't explain. Use it within an ANSI Z133 program and only after proper training.

faq.q: Can I use it for rigging wood?
faq.a: No. It is a climbing connector with a small wheel. Use rated rigging pulleys and blocks for lowering wood.

faq.q: Does it come non-locking?
faq.a: DMM makes non-locking and locking versions. Use a locking version for any life-support connection.

name: DMM Rhino Carabiner
title: DMM Rhino Locking Carabiner
meta: The DMM Rhino is a locking carabiner for heavy-use climbing and rigging connections. Where tree workers use it, how to load it correctly and what to inspect.
tagline: A tough locking DMM carabiner for demanding climbing and rigging connections.
summary: The DMM Rhino carabiner is a locking connector built for demanding work on climbing and rope systems. Tree crews use it where they want a strong, durable carabiner for anchors and connections that see repeated loading.
highlights: Locking gate
Built for demanding connections
Useful for anchors and system connections
Made by DMM in Wales

body.h: Using the Rhino on the job
p: Some connections take more abuse than others: anchor points, connections near the trunk, and anywhere a carabiner rubs bark or hardware. A durable connector like the Rhino is a good fit there. Check the shape, gate and strength markings on the spine to choose the role it will play in your system.

If you are not sure which DMM carabiner fits a job, start by thinking about what it will connect: rope, sling, device or ring. That tells you what shape and size you need, and the gate type follows from whether it is a life-support connection.
Compare sizes and gate styles with our other auto-locking carabiners.
Load along the spine, avoid loading across the gate, and do not allow it to lever over an edge. Make sure the gate locks fully before you weight it.

Treat it as life-support gear: follow the manufacturer's instructions, check it before every climb, and retire it after a hard fall, a drop onto a hard surface, or any damage you can't explain. Use it within an ANSI Z133 program and only after proper training.

faq.q: Is the Rhino steel or aluminum?
faq.a: Check the listing and spine markings for the version you buy.

faq.q: Can I use it for rigging?
faq.a: Only within its marked ratings and DMM's instructions. Keep climbing and rigging gear separate when possible.

name: ISC Aluminum Oval Carabiner
title: ISC Aluminum Oval Carabiner
meta: The ISC aluminum oval carabiner is a symmetric locking oval for pulleys, devices and racking. Where an oval fits on a climbing rig, plus inspection and care.
tagline: A light, symmetric locking oval for pulleys, devices and racking gear.
summary: The ISC aluminum oval carabiner is a symmetric locking connector that keeps pulleys and devices centered. It is a light, versatile carabiner for climbers who build haul systems, carry spare hardware or need an even-loading connector.
highlights: Symmetric oval shape
Light aluminum body
Auto-locking gate
Keeps pulleys and devices centered

p: An oval spreads load evenly between both sides, so pulleys and rope grabs stay centered instead of sliding toward the gate. That makes the ISC oval a solid pick for mechanical advantage setups, racking several pieces of hardware, or pairing with a micro pulley on a climbing system.

Ovals are also common in rescue kits, where pulleys and rope grabs need to stay centered for a haul system to work well. If your crew keeps an aerial rescue kit, a few matching ovals make it quicker to build a system under pressure.
Ovals are generally not as strong as a D of the same weight. Check the spine markings and compare with our other auto-locking carabiners.
Check the gate action and lock each time you clip it, and look for grooves where rope runs. Rinse off grit and sap and dry it before storage.

Treat it as life-support gear: follow the manufacturer's instructions, check it before every climb, and retire it after a hard fall, a drop onto a hard surface, or any damage you can't explain. Use it within an ANSI Z133 program and only after proper training.

faq.q: Is it good for a climbing hitch?
faq.a: It can work, but many climbers prefer a D or HMS for a hitch. Ovals are best for pulleys and devices.

faq.q: Does it auto-lock?
faq.a: It is listed with our auto-locking carabiners. Confirm the gate style on the exact version you buy.

name: ISC Iron Wizard Supersafe Carabiner
title: ISC Iron Wizard Supersafe Carabiner
meta: The ISC Iron Wizard Supersafe carabiner is a durable auto-locking connector for high-wear spots on tree climbing systems. Where it fits and what to inspect.
tagline: A durable ISC auto-locker for high-wear spots on your climbing system.
summary: The ISC Iron Wizard Supersafe carabiner is a durable auto-locking connector for the high-wear points on a climbing system. It pairs a hard-wearing body with ISC's Supersafe gate that needs deliberate action to open.
highlights: Durable body for high-wear connections
Supersafe auto-locking gate
Good where rope or hardware wears connectors
Made by ISC

p: Some connectors on a climbing system see constant rope movement or rub against steel hardware, and aluminum wears through faster there. A tougher carabiner like the Iron Wizard is a good choice for a rope wrench tether, a connection to a steel ring, or an anchor that sees daily use.

A tougher connector is also worth having where carabiners rub against each other, such as at a ring on a bridge or a steel anchor. Aluminum wears quickly against steel, and a worn spot can become a sharp edge that damages rope or slings.
Check the material and strength markings on the spine for the version you buy. See our other auto-locking carabiners for lighter options.
Open and release the gate to confirm it closes and locks every time. Look for wear grooves, cracks and corrosion, and keep it clean and dry.

Treat it as life-support gear: follow the manufacturer's instructions, check it before every climb, and retire it after a hard fall, a drop onto a hard surface, or any damage you can't explain. Use it within an ANSI Z133 program and only after proper training.

faq.q: Is the Iron Wizard steel?
faq.a: The name points to a steel body, but check the spine markings and listing to confirm the material.

faq.q: What is the Supersafe gate?
faq.a: It is ISC's auto-locking gate that needs more than one deliberate motion to open. See ISC's instructions for the sequence.

name: Petzl Bm'D Carabiner
title: Petzl Bm'D Locking Carabiner
meta: The Petzl Bm'D is a light asymmetric D locking carabiner for connecting devices and lanyards. Gate options, where it fits on a tree climbing saddle, and care.
tagline: A light asymmetric D locker for devices, lanyards and bridge connections.
summary: The Petzl Bm'D carabiner is a light, asymmetric D-shaped locking connector with an I-beam profile. Tree climbers use it to attach devices, lanyards and pulleys where a compact, strong carabiner fits best.
highlights: Asymmetric D shape
Light aluminum with an I-beam profile
Available with auto-locking gate options
Good for devices, lanyards and bridges

p: The asymmetric D shape keeps load near the spine and leaves a wide gate opening for clipping devices and rope eyes. Arborists use the Bm'D to attach a mechanical device to a bridge, connect a lanyard to the saddle, or pair with a pulley in a hitch system.

Many climbers keep several Bm'D carabiners on their saddle for different jobs, using color or tape to tell them apart. Keeping your system consistent makes it easier to spot a problem during a pre-climb check.
Petzl offers the Bm'D with different locking gates, including auto-locking versions. Check the gate on the version you choose and compare with our other auto-locking carabiners.
Make sure the gate closes and locks on its own before every climb. Look for grooves, cracks, burrs or a sticky gate and clean it with warm water if needed.

Treat it as life-support gear: follow the manufacturer's instructions, check it before every climb, and retire it after a hard fall, a drop onto a hard surface, or any damage you can't explain. Use it within an ANSI Z133 program and only after proper training.

faq.q: Which gate version should I buy?
faq.a: For life-support connections on a climbing system, most arborists choose an auto-locking gate such as TRIACT-LOCK.

faq.q: Is it big enough for my hitch?
faq.a: It works for many hitch setups, but an HMS gives more room for wide hitches and multiple ropes.

name: Petzl ROLLCLIP Pulley Carabiner
title: Petzl ROLLCLIP Pulley Carabiner
meta: The Petzl ROLLCLIP is a locking carabiner with a built-in pulley for hitch tending, redirects and haul systems. How arborists use it, plus care and inspection.
tagline: A locking carabiner with a built-in pulley for tending a hitch and hauling.
summary: The Petzl ROLLCLIP pulley carabiner puts a pulley wheel inside a locking carabiner, so rope runs smoothly over a sheave. It is a compact way to tend a friction hitch, set a redirect or build a haul system without carrying a separate pulley.
highlights: Built-in pulley in a locking carabiner
Smooth rope running for hitch tending
Useful for redirects and haul systems
Compact, one-piece design

p: On a hitch climbing system, the ROLLCLIP sits below the hitch and lets you pull slack through smoothly with one hand. It also works as a redirect on a stationary rope, or as the moving pulley in a simple 3:1 for tensioning a line or hauling gear.
The ROLLCLIP is also handy in aerial rescue kits, where a quick redirect or haul can make a difference. Practice with it during training so you can set it up without thinking when you need it.
Because the pulley and carabiner are one piece, there is less to clip and nothing to drop. See our other auto-locking carabiners for standard connectors.
Check that the wheel turns freely, the gate closes and locks, and there are no cracks or sharp edges. Rinse out grit and sap after dirty jobs.

Treat it as life-support gear: follow the manufacturer's instructions, check it before every climb, and retire it after a hard fall, a drop onto a hard surface, or any damage you can't explain. Use it within an ANSI Z133 program and only after proper training.

faq.q: Can I use it to rig wood?
faq.a: No. It is a climbing and rescue pulley carabiner. Use rated rigging blocks and pulleys for lowering wood.

faq.q: Which version should I buy?
faq.a: Petzl makes more than one ROLLCLIP version. Choose the gate style and markings your employer requires.

name: Rock Exotica rockO Orca Lock Carabiner
keyword: rock exotica rocko orca lock carabiner
title: Rock Exotica rockO Orca Lock Carabiner
h1: Rock Exotica rockO Orca Lock Carabiner
meta: The Rock Exotica rockO with Orca lock is a large aluminum auto-locking carabiner for anchors, devices and lanyards. Where it fits and how to inspect it daily.
tagline: A roomy aluminum auto-locker with Rock Exotica's Orca locking gate.
summary: The Rock Exotica rockO Orca Lock carabiner is a large, roomy aluminum connector with an auto-locking Orca gate. Its size and smooth gate make it popular for anchors, devices and lanyard connections on climbing and rescue systems.
highlights: Large, roomy aluminum carabiner
Orca auto-locking gate
Good for anchors, devices and lanyards
Made in the USA by Rock Exotica

p: The rockO has a big basket and a generous gate opening, so it clips large eye splices, rings and device attachment points without fuss. Arborists use it as a master carabiner on an anchor, to attach SRS devices, or to connect a lanyard to a saddle.
When choosing between carabiners, think about how often you clip and unclip it. A large, smooth-opening carabiner like the rockO makes repeated clipping easier on cold days and with gloves on.
The Orca gate locks automatically and is designed to open smoothly with gloves on. Compare it with our other auto-locking carabiners.
Check that the gate snaps shut and locks every time. Look for wear grooves, cracks, burrs or corrosion and keep it free of sap and grit.

Treat it as life-support gear: follow the manufacturer's instructions, check it before every climb, and retire it after a hard fall, a drop onto a hard surface, or any damage you can't explain. Use it within an ANSI Z133 program and only after proper training.

faq.q: Is it good for SRS devices?
faq.a: Many climbers use it to attach SRS devices. Confirm compatibility in the device maker's instructions.

faq.q: What makes the Orca lock different?
faq.a: It is Rock Exotica's auto-locking gate style. See Rock Exotica's instructions for how to open and close it.

name: Rock Exotica rockO Wire Eye Carabiner
title: Rock Exotica rockO Wire Eye Carabiner
h1: Rock Exotica rockO Wire Eye Carabiner
meta: The Rock Exotica rockO Wire Eye carabiner adds a captive eye to keep a sling, eye or device in place. Where it helps on a climbing system and what to check.
tagline: A rockO carabiner with a captive eye that keeps a connection in position.
summary: The Rock Exotica rockO Wire Eye carabiner is a rockO auto-locker with a captive wire eye that holds an attached eye, sling or device in one spot. That helps keep the connection oriented so it does not rotate onto the gate.
highlights: Captive eye holds connections in place
Large rockO aluminum body
Auto-locking gate
Helps prevent cross-loading

p: A sling, rope eye or device can migrate around a carabiner as you move, ending up on the gate or across the minor axis. The captive eye on this rockO keeps one connection fixed at the spine end, so the carabiner stays oriented when you climb, rig a bridge or set a lanyard.

A captive eye is especially useful on lanyard ends and device attachments, where the connection is clipped and unclipped often. Keeping it fixed means one less thing to check each time you reposition.
Check Rock Exotica's instructions for what can be captured and how. Compare it with our other auto-locking carabiners.
Check the wire eye for kinks, fraying or a loose fit, and confirm the gate locks fully. Keep it clean of sap and grit.

Treat it as life-support gear: follow the manufacturer's instructions, check it before every climb, and retire it after a hard fall, a drop onto a hard surface, or any damage you can't explain. Use it within an ANSI Z133 program and only after proper training.

faq.q: What goes in the captive eye?
faq.a: Follow Rock Exotica's instructions. It is meant to hold one connection in place at the spine end.

faq.q: Can I remove the wire eye?
faq.a: Only if the manufacturer's instructions allow it. Do not modify life-support hardware.

name: DMM Prest-In Grommet
title: DMM Prest-In Grommet Carabiner Keeper
meta: The DMM Prest-In grommet holds a carabiner in position on a sling, eye or attachment point. How a carabiner keeper helps your system and what to watch for.
tagline: A small keeper that holds a carabiner in the right position on a sling or eye.
summary: The DMM Prest-In grommet is a small keeper that holds a carabiner in place on a sling, eye or attachment point. Keeping the carabiner oriented reduces the chance of it rotating onto the gate or loading across the minor axis.
highlights: Holds a carabiner in position
Helps prevent rotation and cross-loading
Small, light configuration aid
Fits slings, eyes and lanyards

p: A carabiner that is free to flip can end up loaded the wrong way. A grommet or keeper holds it in position on a sling or eye so it stays spine-loaded and gate-out. Climbers use keepers on lanyard ends, bridges and device attachments to keep their system tidy and predictable.
Keepers are cheap and small, so it makes sense to have spares in your kit. Replace them when they start to stretch or crack, and check that each one still holds the carabiner firmly in position.

A grommet is not load-bearing. It only holds the carabiner in place; all loads go through the sling and the carabiner.

Check the keeper during your pre-climb inspection, replace it if it is cracked or loose, and make sure it does not interfere with the gate. Fit it according to DMM's instructions and use your system within an ANSI Z133 program.

faq.q: Does it add strength?
faq.a: No. It only holds the carabiner in position and carries no load.

faq.q: Will it fit my carabiner?
faq.a: Check DMM's guidance for compatible carabiner and sling sizes.
